### Clone repository and run initial setup

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/pydantic-core/README.md

Clones the repository and installs dependencies with uv, sets up pre-commit hooks, and builds the development version.

```bash
# Clone the repository (or from your fork)
git clone git@github.com:pydantic/pydantic-core.git
cd pydantic-core

# Install all dependencies using uv, setup pre-commit hooks, and build the development version
make install
```

--------------------------------

### Clone fork and install uv, pre-commit, and dependencies

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/contributing.md

Run after forking the repository on GitHub. Clones your fork, installs uv and pre-commit, then runs `make install` to install pydantic, test, and doc dependencies.

```bash
# Clone your fork and cd into the repo directory
git clone git@github.com:<your username>/pydantic.git
cd pydantic

# Install UV and pre-commit
# We use uv here, for other options see:
# https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/
# https://pre-commit.com/#install
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
uv tool install pre-commit

# Install pydantic, dependencies, test dependencies and doc dependencies
make install
```

### Install pydantic for AWS Lambda with pip

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/integrations/aws_lambda.md

Installs binary wheels compatible with the AWS Lambda runtime into a target directory for deployment packages or Lambda Layers. Customize `--platform` and `--python-version` to match the target Lambda runtime.

```bash
pip install \
    --platform manylinux2014_x86_64 \  # (1)!
    --target=<your_package_dir> \  # (2)!
    --implementation cp \  # (3)!
    --python-version 3.10 \  # (4)!
    --only-binary=:all: \  # (5)!
    --upgrade pydantic  # (6)!
```

### Enable all pydantic-mypy strictness flags in pyproject.toml

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/integrations/mypy.md

Example pyproject.toml configuration that enables the pydantic.mypy plugin and sets all plugin strictness flags to true, along with several mypy strictness flags.

```toml
[tool.mypy]
plugins = ["pydantic.mypy"]

follow_imports = "silent"
warn_redundant_casts = true
warn_unused_ignores = true
disallow_any_generics = true
no_implicit_reexport = true
disallow_untyped_defs = true

[tool.pydantic-mypy]
init_forbid_extra = true
init_typed = true
warn_required_dynamic_aliases = true
```

### Pydantic model data conversion example

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/models.md

Shows how Pydantic casts input values to declared field types, which can lose information. The output demonstrates conversion of float to int, string to float, and bytes to str.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel


class Model(BaseModel):
    a: int
    b: float
    c: str


print(Model(a=3.000, b='2.72', c=b'binary data').model_dump())
#> {'a': 3, 'b': 2.72, 'c': 'binary data'}
```

### Pickle and unpickle a Pydantic model with pickle.dumps and pickle.loads

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/serialization.md

Pydantic models support efficient pickling and unpickling. The example dumps a model, prints the first 20 bytes of the pickled data, then loads it back into an equivalent model.

```python
import pickle

from pydantic import BaseModel


class FooBarModel(BaseModel):
    a: str
    b: int


m = FooBarModel(a='hello', b=123)
print(m)
#> a='hello' b=123
data = pickle.dumps(m)
print(data[:20])
#> b'\x80\x05\x95\x95\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x8c\x08__main_'
m2 = pickle.loads(data)
print(m2)
#> a='hello' b=123
```

### Configure Pydantic dataclasses with ConfigDict

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/config.md

Passes a ConfigDict instance to the config argument of the Pydantic dataclass decorator. This example configures assignment validation and string length limits on dataclass fields.

```python
from pydantic import ConfigDict, ValidationError
from pydantic.dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(config=ConfigDict(str_max_length=10, validate_assignment=True))
class User:
    name: str


user = User(name='John Doe')
try:
    user.name = 'x' * 20
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e)
    """
    1 validation error for User
    name
      String should have at most 10 characters [type=string_too_long, input_value='xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx', input_type=str]
    """
```

### Encountering missing pydantic_core module error

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/integrations/aws_lambda.md

Indicates that Pydantic was installed incorrectly for the target Lambda environment. Run debugging steps before the failing import to diagnose native extension or Python version mismatches.

```output
no module named `pydantic_core._pydantic_core`
```

type A = A

### Dump a model with JSON-compatible types using model_dump(mode='json')

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/serialization.md

Set mode='json' on model_dump() to ensure JSON-compatible types are used; for example, tuples are converted to lists.

```python
print(m.model_dump(mode='json'))
#> {'banana': 3.14, 'foo': 'hello', 'bar': {'whatever': [1, 2]}}
```

### Example Pydantic model with type errors

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/integrations/mypy.md

This script defines a Pydantic model with an untyped field and passes arguments of incorrect types. It is used to demonstrate mypy's behavior with and without the Pydantic plugin.

```python
from datetime import datetime

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Model(BaseModel):
    age: int
    first_name = 'John'
    last_name: str | None = None
    signup_ts: datetime | None = None
    list_of_ints: list[int]


m = Model(age=42, list_of_ints=[1, '2', b'3'])
print(m.middle_name)  # not a model field!
Model()  # will raise a validation error for age and list_of_ints
```

### Customize Field JSON Schema Attributes

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/json_schema.md

Customizes field schema metadata such as description, title, examples, and additional properties via json_schema_extra using Field() and Annotated.

```python
import json
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field, SecretStr


class User(BaseModel):
    age: int = Field(description='Age of the user')
    email: Annotated[EmailStr, Field(examples=['marcelo@mail.com'])]  # (1)!
    name: str = Field(title='Username')
    password: SecretStr = Field(
        json_schema_extra={
            'title': 'Password',
            'description': 'Password of the user',
            'examples': ['123456'],
        }
    )


print(json.dumps(User.model_json_schema(), indent=2))
"""
{
  "properties": {
    "age": {
      "description": "Age of the user",
      "title": "Age",
      "type": "integer"
    },
    "email": {
      "examples": [
        "marcelo@mail.com"
      ],
      "format": "email",
      "title": "Email",
      "type": "string"
    },
    "name": {
      "title": "Username",
      "type": "string"
    },
    "password": {
      "description": "Password of the user",
      "examples": [
        "123456"
      ],
      "format": "password",
      "title": "Password",
      "type": "string",
      "writeOnly": true
    }
  },
  "required": [
    "age",
    "email",
    "name",
    "password"
  ],
  "title": "User",
  "type": "object"
}
"""
```

### Define and validate a Pydantic model

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/README.md

Use BaseModel to define a model with typed fields. Instantiate it with external data to validate and coerce types; the example prints the model and its id field.

```python
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel

class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str = 'John Doe'
    signup_ts: Optional[datetime] = None
    friends: list[int] = []

external_data = {'id': '123', 'signup_ts': '2017-06-01 12:22', 'friends': [1, '2', b'3']}
user = User(**external_data)
print(user)
#> User id=123 name='John Doe' signup_ts=datetime.datetime(2017, 6, 1, 12, 22) friends=[1, 2, 3]
print(user.id)
#> 123
```

### Resolving annotations with explicit _types_namespace

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/internals/resolving_annotations.md

Shows an example where providing an explicit _types_namespace fails to find parent function-scoped variables, raising PydanticUndefinedAnnotation.

```python
def func():
    A = list[int]

    class Model(BaseModel):
        f: 'A | Forward'

    return Model


Model = func()

Model.model_rebuild(_types_namespace={'Forward': str})
# pydantic.errors.PydanticUndefinedAnnotation: name 'A' is not defined
```

### Configuring nested Pydantic models with model_config boundaries

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/config.md

Configuration does not propagate into nested Pydantic models and dataclasses because each model maintains its own configuration boundary. In this example, Parent's str_to_lower=True does not affect the nested User model.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict


class User(BaseModel):
    name: str


class Parent(BaseModel):
    user: User

    model_config = ConfigDict(str_to_lower=True)


print(Parent(user={'name': 'JOHN'}))
#> user=User(name='JOHN')
```

### Validate data with model_validate, model_validate_json, and model_validate_strings

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/models.md

Use model_validate for Python dicts, model_validate_json for JSON strings, and model_validate_strings for string-keyed dicts. The example shows successful validation, a JSON type error, and strict mode rejecting a date-only string for a datetime field.

```python
from datetime import datetime

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError


class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str = 'John Doe'
    signup_ts: datetime | None = None


m = User.model_validate({'id': 123, 'name': 'James'})
print(m)
#> id=123 name='James' signup_ts=None

try:
    m = User.model_validate_json('{"id": 123, "name": 123}')
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e)
    """
    1 validation error for User
    name
      Input should be a valid string [type=string_type, input_value=123, input_type=int]
    """

m = User.model_validate_strings({'id': '123', 'name': 'James'})
print(m)
#> id=123 name='James' signup_ts=None

m = User.model_validate_strings(
    {'id': '123', 'name': 'James', 'signup_ts': '2024-04-01T12:00:00'}
)
print(m)
#> id=123 name='James' signup_ts=datetime.datetime(2024, 4, 1, 12, 0)

try:
    m = User.model_validate_strings(
        {'id': '123', 'name': 'James', 'signup_ts': '2024-04-01'}, strict=True
    )
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e)
    """
    1 validation error for User
    signup_ts
      Input should be a valid datetime, invalid datetime separator, expected `T`, `t`, `_` or space [type=datetime_parsing, input_value='2024-04-01', input_type=str]
    """

```

### Create a dynamic model with create_model and compare to static class

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/models.md

Use create_model() to build a model at runtime from field definitions. Field definitions are keyword arguments: a single type or a two-tuple of (type, default/Field).

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, create_model

DynamicFoobarModel = create_model('DynamicFoobarModel', foo=str, bar=(int, 123))

# Equivalent to:


class StaticFoobarModel(BaseModel):
    foo: str
    bar: int = 123
```

### Customize Generated JSON Schema with __get_pydantic_json_schema__

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/json_schema.md

Implement __get_pydantic_json_schema__ to modify generated JSON schema metadata such as examples and titles. This customization affects only the JSON schema output and leaves core validation intact.

```python
import json
from typing import Any

from pydantic_core import core_schema as cs

from pydantic import GetCoreSchemaHandler, GetJsonSchemaHandler, TypeAdapter
from pydantic.json_schema import JsonSchemaValue


class Person:
    name: str
    age: int

    def __init__(self, name: str, age: int):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

    @classmethod
    def __get_pydantic_core_schema__(
        cls, source_type: Any, handler: GetCoreSchemaHandler
    ) -> cs.CoreSchema:
        return cs.typed_dict_schema(
            {
                'name': cs.typed_dict_field(cs.str_schema()),
                'age': cs.typed_dict_field(cs.int_schema()),
            },
        )

    @classmethod
    def __get_pydantic_json_schema__(
        cls, core_schema: cs.CoreSchema, handler: GetJsonSchemaHandler
    ) -> JsonSchemaValue:
        json_schema = handler(core_schema)
        json_schema = handler.resolve_ref_schema(json_schema)
        json_schema['examples'] = [
            {
                'name': 'John Doe',
                'age': 25,
            }
        ]
        json_schema['title'] = 'Person'
        return json_schema


print(json.dumps(TypeAdapter(Person).json_schema(), indent=2))
"""
{
  "examples": [
    {
      "age": 25,
      "name": "John Doe"
    }
  ],
  "properties": {
    "name": {
      "title": "Name",
      "type": "string"
    },
    "age": {
      "title": "Age",
      "type": "integer"
    }
  },
  "required": [
    "name",
    "age"
  ],
  "title": "Person",
  "type": "object"
}
"""
```

### Rebuild TypeAdapter schema with defer_build and rebuild()

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/type_adapter.md

Defers core schema building using ConfigDict(defer_build=True) for a forward reference and manually triggers schema generation using ta.rebuild() once the type is defined.

```python
from pydantic import ConfigDict, TypeAdapter

ta = TypeAdapter('MyInt', config=ConfigDict(defer_build=True))

# some time later, the forward reference is defined
MyInt = int

ta.rebuild()
assert ta.validate_python(1) == 1

```

--------------------------------

### Define model_post_init to run logic after model initialization

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/models.md

Use model_post_init instead of a custom __init__ to perform actions after initialization while preserving validation parameters. The method receives the validation context and runs after the model is initialized.

```python
import logging
from typing import Any

from pydantic import BaseModel


class MyModel(BaseModel):
    id: int

    def model_post_init(self, context: Any) -> None:
        logging.info("Model initialized with id %d", self.id)
```

### Trigger assertion_error with a failing field_validator assert

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/errors/validation_errors.md

A failing assert inside a field_validator raises an assertion_error during validation. The example prints the error type from the first error.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError, field_validator


class Model(BaseModel):
    x: int

    @field_validator('x')
    @classmethod
    def force_x_positive(cls, v):
        assert v > 0
        return v


try:
    Model(x=-1)
except ValidationError as exc:
    print(repr(exc.errors()[0]['type']))
    #> 'assertion_error'
```

### Provide context during direct model instantiation using ContextVar

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/validators.md

Work around direct `Model(...)` instantiation context limitations by storing context in a `ContextVar` and intercepting initialization in a custom `__init__` method.

```python
from __future__ import annotations

from collections.abc import Generator
from contextlib import contextmanager
from contextvars import ContextVar
from typing import Any

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationInfo, field_validator

_init_context_var = ContextVar('_init_context_var', default=None)


@contextmanager
def init_context(value: dict[str, Any]) -> Generator[None]:
    token = _init_context_var.set(value)
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        _init_context_var.reset(token)


class Model(BaseModel):
    my_number: int

    def __init__(self, /, **data: Any) -> None:
        self.__pydantic_validator__.validate_python(
            data,
            self_instance=self,
            context=_init_context_var.get(),
        )

    @field_validator('my_number')
    @classmethod
    def multiply_with_context(cls, value: int, info: ValidationInfo) -> int:
        if isinstance(info.context, dict):
            multiplier = info.context.get('multiplier', 1)
            value = value * multiplier
        return value


print(Model(my_number=2))
#> my_number=2

with init_context({'multiplier': 3}):
    print(Model(my_number=2))
    #> my_number=6

print(Model(my_number=2))
#> my_number=2
```

### Field Serializer with Serialization Info

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/serialization.md

A field serializer can optionally accept an `info` argument of type `FieldSerializationInfo`, which provides access to the serialization context, mode, and other parameters. This example shows a field serializer that uses the context to remove stopwords from a string field.

```APIDOC
## Field Serializer with Serialization Info

### Description
A field serializer can optionally accept an `info` argument of type `FieldSerializationInfo`, which provides access to the serialization context, mode, and other parameters. This example shows a field serializer that uses the context to remove stopwords from a string field.

### Method
`@field_serializer` decorator

### Parameters
#### Serializer Function Parameters
- **v** (str) - Required - The field value to serialize.
- **info** (FieldSerializationInfo) - Optional - Provides extra information such as `context`, `mode`, and `field_name`.

### Request Example
```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, FieldSerializationInfo, field_serializer

class Model(BaseModel):
    text: str

    @field_serializer('text', mode='plain')
    @classmethod
    def remove_stopwords(cls, v: str, info: FieldSerializationInfo) -> str:
        if isinstance(info.context, dict):
            stopwords = info.context.get('stopwords', set())
            v = ' '.join(w for w in v.split() if w.lower() not in stopwords)
        return v

model = Model(text='This is an example document')
print(model.model_dump())  # no context
#> {'text': 'This is an example document'}
print(model.model_dump(context={'stopwords': ['this', 'is', 'an']}))
#> {'text': 'example document'}
```

### Response
#### Success Response
- **dict** - The serialized model data.

#### Response Example
```python
{'text': 'example document'}
```
```

### Add validators and computed fields via __namespace__ in create_model

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/models.md

Use __namespace__ to add validators, computed fields, or methods to a dynamically created model. Namespace keys must not clash with field names; the example shows a validation error for a non-alphanumeric first_name.

```python
from pydantic import (
    ValidationError,
    computed_field,
    create_model,
    field_validator,
)


def alphanum(cls, v: str) -> str:
    assert v.isalnum(), 'must be alphanumeric'
    return v


def full_name(self) -> str:
    return f'{self.first_name} {self.last_name}'


UserModel = create_model(
    'UserModel',
    first_name=str,
    last_name=str,
    __namespace__={  # (1)!
        'check_alphanum': field_validator('first_name', 'last_name')(alphanum),
        'full_name': computed_field(property(full_name)),
    },
)

user = UserModel(first_name='John', last_name='Doe')
print(user.model_dump())
#> {'first_name': 'John', 'last_name': 'Doe', 'full_name': 'John Doe'}

try:
    UserModel(first_name='J%hn', last_name='Doe')
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e)
    """
    1 validation error for UserModel
    first_name
      Assertion failed, must be alphanumeric [type=assertion_error, input_value='J%hn', input_type=str]
    """
```

### Create a generic model with PEP 695 type parameter syntax (Python 3.12+)

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/models.md

Use the new type parameter syntax to declare a generic Response model with DataT as a type parameter. Requires Python 3.12+; parametrizing with a concrete type validates data and raises ValidationError on invalid input.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError


class DataModel(BaseModel):
    number: int


class Response[DataT](BaseModel):  # (1)!
    data: DataT  # (2)!


print(Response[int](data=1))
#> data=1
print(Response[str](data='value'))
#> data='value'
print(Response[str](data='value').model_dump())
#> {'data': 'value'}

data = DataModel(number=1)
print(Response[DataModel](data=data).model_dump())
#> {'data': {'number': 1}}
try:
    Response[int](data='value')
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e)
    """
    1 validation error for Response[int]
    data
      Input should be a valid integer, unable to parse string as an integer [type=int_parsing, input_value='value', input_type=str]
    """
```

### Preserve field order in model_fields, model_dump, and validation errors

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/models.md

Field order is preserved in JSON Schema, validation errors, and serialization, and fields are validated in order. The example shows model_fields keys, model_dump output, and error locations for a model with defaults.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError


class Model(BaseModel):
    a: int
    b: int = 2
    c: int = 1
    d: int = 0
    e: float


print(Model.model_fields.keys())
#> dict_keys(['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e'])
m = Model(e=2, a=1)
print(m.model_dump())
#> {'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'c': 1, 'd': 0, 'e': 2.0}
try:
    Model(a='x', b='x', c='x', d='x', e='x')
except ValidationError as err:
    error_locations = [e['loc'] for e in err.errors()]

print(error_locations)
#> [('a',), ('b',), ('c',), ('d',), ('e',)]
```

### Mapping BeforeValidator, AfterValidator, and WrapValidator with pipeline API

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/experimental.md

Demonstrates type-safe equivalents for `BeforeValidator`, `AfterValidator`, and `WrapValidator` behaviors using `validate_as` and `transform`.

```python
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic.experimental.pipeline import transform, validate_as

# BeforeValidator
Annotated[int, validate_as(str).str_strip().validate_as(...)]  # (1)!
# AfterValidator
Annotated[int, transform(lambda x: x * 2)]  # (2)!
# WrapValidator
Annotated[
    int,
    validate_as(str)
    .str_strip()
    .validate_as(...)
    .transform(lambda x: x * 2),  # (3)!
]
```

### Field alias takes precedence over alias_generator

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/alias.md

When an explicit alias is set on a Field, it overrides the alias generated by alias_generator by default. The example shows validation using the explicit alias 'lang' and serialization with by_alias=True.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field


def to_camel(string: str) -> str:
    return ''.join(word.capitalize() for word in string.split('_'))


class Voice(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(alias_generator=to_camel)

    name: str
    language_code: str = Field(alias='lang')


voice = Voice(Name='Filiz', lang='tr-TR')
print(voice.language_code)
#> tr-TR
print(voice.model_dump(by_alias=True))
#> {'Name': 'Filiz', 'lang': 'tr-TR'}
```

### Benchmark JSON parsing and URL validation with TypeAdapter vs pure Python

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/why.md

Benchmark parsing JSON and validating URLs using pure Python versus Pydantic's TypeAdapter. Demonstrates validation speedups powered by pydantic-core Rust implementation.

```python
import json
import timeit
from urllib.parse import urlparse

import requests

from pydantic import HttpUrl, TypeAdapter

reps = 7
number = 100
r = requests.get('https://api.github.com/emojis')
r.raise_for_status()
emojis_json = r.content


def emojis_pure_python(raw_data):
    data = json.loads(raw_data)
    output = {}
    for key, value in data.items():
        assert isinstance(key, str)
        url = urlparse(value)
        assert url.scheme in ('https', 'http')
        output[key] = url


emojis_pure_python_times = timeit.repeat(
    'emojis_pure_python(emojis_json)',
    globals={
        'emojis_pure_python': emojis_pure_python,
        'emojis_json': emojis_json,
    },
    repeat=reps,
    number=number,
)
print(f'pure python: {min(emojis_pure_python_times) / number * 1000:0.2f}ms')
#> pure python: 5.32ms

type_adapter = TypeAdapter(dict[str, HttpUrl])
emojis_pydantic_times = timeit.repeat(
    'type_adapter.validate_json(emojis_json)',
    globals={
        'type_adapter': type_adapter,
        'HttpUrl': HttpUrl,
        'emojis_json': emojis_json,
    },
    repeat=reps,
    number=number,
)
print(f'pydantic: {min(emojis_pydantic_times) / number * 1000:0.2f}ms')
#> pydantic: 1.54ms

print(
    f'Pydantic {min(emojis_pure_python_times) / min(emojis_pydantic_times):0.2f}x faster'
)
#> Pydantic 3.45x faster
```

### Use serialize_as_any runtime setting in model_dump()

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/serialization.md

Pass serialize_as_any=True to model_dump() to include subclass fields; with False (the V2 default), fields present only on the subclass are excluded from serialization.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel


class User(BaseModel):
    name: str


class UserLogin(User):
    password: str


class OuterModel(BaseModel):
    user1: User
    user2: User


user = UserLogin(name='pydantic', password='password')

outer_model = OuterModel(user1=user, user2=user)
print(outer_model.model_dump(serialize_as_any=True))  # (1)!
"""
{
    'user1': {'name': 'pydantic', 'password': 'password'},
    'user2': {'name': 'pydantic', 'password': 'password'},
}
"""

print(outer_model.model_dump(serialize_as_any=False))  # (2)!
#> {'user1': {'name': 'pydantic'}, 'user2': {'name': 'pydantic'}}

```

### Raise needs_python_object validation error when validating from JSON

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/errors/validation_errors.md

Raises a 'needs_python_object' error when validation is attempted from a format that cannot be converted to a Python object, such as checking isinstance/issubclass from JSON. The example prints the error type from the caught ValidationError.

```python
import json

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError


class Model(BaseModel):
    bm: type[BaseModel]


try:
    Model.model_validate_json(json.dumps({'bm': 'not a basemodel class'}))
except ValidationError as exc:
    print(repr(exc.errors()[0]['type']))
    #> 'needs_python_object'
```

### Transforming data using UserIn and UserOut models

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/experimental.md

Shows an alternative plain Python pattern using separate `UserIn` and `UserOut` models instead of complex pipeline type annotations.

```python
from __future__ import annotations

from pydantic import BaseModel


class UserIn(BaseModel):
    favorite_number: int | str


class UserOut(BaseModel):
    favorite_number: int


def my_api(user: UserIn) -> UserOut:
    favorite_number = user.favorite_number
    if isinstance(favorite_number, str):
        favorite_number = int(user.favorite_number.strip())

    return UserOut(favorite_number=favorite_number)


assert my_api(UserIn(favorite_number=' 1 ')).favorite_number == 1
```

### Advanced create_model with Field, Annotated, and PrivateAttr

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/models.md

Shows field definitions using Field(alias=...), Annotated with Field(description=...), and PrivateAttr for private attributes. The static class shows the equivalent declarations.

```python
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, PrivateAttr, create_model

DynamicModel = create_model(
    'DynamicModel',
    foo=(str, Field(alias='FOO')),
    bar=Annotated[str, Field(description='Bar field')],
    _private=(int, PrivateAttr(default=1)),
)


class StaticModel(BaseModel):
    foo: str = Field(alias='FOO')
    bar: Annotated[str, Field(description='Bar field')]
    _private: int = PrivateAttr(default=1)
```

### Propagating configuration to standard library dataclasses with with_config override

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/config.md

Configuration propagates down to standard library dataclasses and typed dictionaries unless the type defines its own configuration. Here, user_1 inherits str_to_lower=True while user_2 overrides it with @with_config(str_to_lower=False).

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, with_config


@dataclass
class UserWithoutConfig:
    name: str


@dataclass
@with_config(str_to_lower=False)
class UserWithConfig:
    name: str


class Parent(BaseModel):
    user_1: UserWithoutConfig
    user_2: UserWithConfig

    model_config = ConfigDict(str_to_lower=True)


print(Parent(user_1={'name': 'JOHN'}, user_2={'name': 'JOHN'}))
#> user_1=UserWithoutConfig(name='john') user_2=UserWithConfig(name='JOHN')
```

### Use __future__.annotations for Forward References in Python 3.13 and Lower

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/forward_annotations.md

Use `from __future__ import annotations` (or quote annotations manually) in Python versions prior to 3.14 to reference types defined later in the file.

```python
from __future__ import annotations

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Model(BaseModel):
    a: MyInt
    # Without the future import, equivalent to:
    # a: 'MyInt'


MyInt = int


print(Model(a='1'))
#> a=1
```

### Customizing core schema with __get_pydantic_core_schema__ and Annotated

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/internals/architecture.md

Applies custom metadata wrappers using __get_pydantic_core_schema__ to modify core schemas recursively via GetCoreSchemaHandler.

```python
from typing import Annotated, Any

from pydantic_core import CoreSchema

from pydantic import GetCoreSchemaHandler, TypeAdapter


class MyStrict:
    @classmethod
    def __get_pydantic_core_schema__(
        cls, source: Any, handler: GetCoreSchemaHandler
    ) -> CoreSchema:
        schema = handler(source)  # (1)!
        schema['strict'] = True
        return schema


class MyGt:
    @classmethod
    def __get_pydantic_core_schema__(
        cls, source: Any, handler: GetCoreSchemaHandler
    ) -> CoreSchema:
        schema = handler(source)  # (2)!
        schema['gt'] = 1
        return schema


ta = TypeAdapter(Annotated[int, MyStrict(), MyGt()])
```

### Configure dataclass fields with Field parameters

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/fields.md

Apply Field() parameters such as init_var and kw_only to Pydantic dataclasses. Init-only fields (init_var=True) are passed to initialization but excluded from serialized output like model_dump().

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from pydantic.dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Foo:
    bar: str
    baz: str = Field(init_var=True)
    qux: str = Field(kw_only=True)


class Model(BaseModel):
    foo: Foo


model = Model(foo=Foo('bar', baz='baz', qux='qux'))
print(model.model_dump())  # (1)!
#> {'foo': {'bar': 'bar', 'qux': 'qux'}}
```

### Perform Partial Validation with TypeAdapter

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/experimental.md

Demonstrates validating incomplete JSON strings and Python objects using TypeAdapter.validate_json and TypeAdapter.validate_python with experimental_allow_partial set to True or 'trailing-strings'.

```python
from typing import Annotated

from annotated_types import MinLen
from typing_extensions import NotRequired, TypedDict

from pydantic import TypeAdapter


class Foobar(TypedDict):  # (1)!
    a: int
    b: NotRequired[float]
    c: NotRequired[Annotated[str, MinLen(5)]]


ta = TypeAdapter(list[Foobar])

v = ta.validate_json('[{"a": 1, "b"', experimental_allow_partial=True)  # (2)!
print(v)
#> [{'a': 1}]

v = ta.validate_json(
    '[{"a": 1, "b": 1.0, "c": "abcd', experimental_allow_partial=True  # (3)!
)
print(v)
#> [{'a': 1, 'b': 1.0}]

v = ta.validate_json(
    '[{"b": 1.0, "c": "abcde"', experimental_allow_partial=True  # (4)!
)
print(v)
#> []

v = ta.validate_json(
    '[{"a": 1, "b": 1.0, "c": "abcde"},{"a": ', experimental_allow_partial=True
)
print(v)
#> [{'a': 1, 'b': 1.0, 'c': 'abcde'}]

v = ta.validate_python([{'a': 1}], experimental_allow_partial=True)  # (5)!
print(v)
#> [{'a': 1}]

v = ta.validate_python(
    [{'a': 1, 'b': 1.0, 'c': 'abcd'}], experimental_allow_partial=True  # (6)!
)
print(v)
#> [{'a': 1, 'b': 1.0}]

v = ta.validate_json(
    '[{"a": 1, "b": 1.0, "c": "abcdefg',
    experimental_allow_partial='trailing-strings',  # (7)!
)
print(v)
#> [{'a': 1, 'b': 1.0, 'c': 'abcdefg'}]
```

### Define generic container types with __get_pydantic_core_schema__

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/types.md

Demonstrates creating a custom generic container type using `get_args` and `handler.generate_schema`. Uses `union_schema` to accept existing instances or validate and wrap incoming sequence data.

```python
from collections.abc import Sequence
from typing import Any, TypeVar, get_args

from pydantic_core import ValidationError, core_schema

from pydantic import BaseModel, GetCoreSchemaHandler

T = TypeVar('T')


class MySequence(Sequence[T]):
    def __init__(self, v: Sequence[T]):
        self.v = v

    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return self.v[i]

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.v)

    @classmethod
    def __get_pydantic_core_schema__(
        cls, source: Any, handler: GetCoreSchemaHandler
    ) -> core_schema.CoreSchema:
        instance_schema = core_schema.is_instance_schema(cls)

        args = get_args(source)
        if args:
            # replace the type and rely on Pydantic to generate the right schema
            # for `Sequence`
            sequence_t_schema = handler.generate_schema(Sequence[args[0]])
        else:
            sequence_t_schema = handler.generate_schema(Sequence)

        non_instance_schema = core_schema.no_info_after_validator_function(
            MySequence, sequence_t_schema
        )
        return core_schema.union_schema([instance_schema, non_instance_schema])


class M(BaseModel):
    model_config = dict(validate_default=True)

    s1: MySequence = [3]


m = M()
print(m)
#> s1=<__main__.MySequence object at 0x0123456789ab>
print(m.s1.v)
#> [3]


class M(BaseModel):
    s1: MySequence[int]


M(s1=[1])
try:
    M(s1=['a'])
except ValidationError as exc:
    print(exc)
    """
    2 validation errors for M
    s1.is-instance[MySequence]
      Input should be an instance of MySequence [type=is_instance_of, input_value=['a'], input_type=list]
    s1.function-after[MySequence(), json-or-python[json=list[int],python=chain[is-instance[Sequence],function-wrap[sequence_validator()]]]].0
      Input should be a valid integer, unable to parse string as an integer [type=int_parsing, input_value='a', input_type=str]
    """
```

### Derive a model with all fields made optional using create_model()

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/examples/dynamic_models.md

Dynamically creates a new model from an existing BaseModel subclass with all fields made optional with a default of None. Setting __base__ inherits validators and computed fields from the parent model.

```python
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, create_model


def make_fields_optional(model_cls: type[BaseModel]) -> type[BaseModel]:
    new_fields = {}

    for f_name, f_info in model_cls.model_fields.items():
        f_dct = f_info.asdict()
        new_fields[f_name] = (
            Annotated[(f_dct['annotation'] | None, *f_dct['metadata'], Field(**f_dct['attributes']))],
            None,
        )

    return create_model(
        f'{model_cls.__name__}Optional',
        __base__=model_cls,  # (1)!
        **new_fields,
    )
```

```python
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, create_model


def make_fields_optional(model_cls: type[BaseModel]) -> type[BaseModel]:
    new_fields = {}

    for f_name, f_info in model_cls.model_fields.items():
        f_dct = f_info.asdict()
        new_fields[f_name] = (
            Annotated[f_dct['annotation'] | None, *f_dct['metadata'], Field(**f_dct['attributes'])],
            None,
        )

    return create_model(
        f'{model_cls.__name__}Optional',
        __base__=model_cls,  # (1)!
        **new_fields,
    )
```

### model_dump(include=...)

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/serialization.md

The `model_dump()` method serializes a model instance to a dictionary. The `include` parameter specifies which fields to include in the output, supporting sets, dictionaries, and nested field specifications. Using `False` to exclude a field in `include` is not supported.

```APIDOC
## model_dump(include=...)

### Description
Serializes the model instance to a dictionary, including only the specified fields. The `include` parameter accepts a set of field names or a dictionary mapping field names to `True` (include entirely) or nested inclusion specifications. Using `False` to exclude a field in `include` is not supported.

### Method
`model_dump()`

### Parameters
- **include** (set[str] | dict) - Optional - Fields to include. Can be a set of field names, or a dict where values are `True` (include the field) or nested dicts/sets for nested models and sequences.

### Example
```python
print(t.model_dump(include={'id': True, 'user': {'id'}}))
#> {'id': '1234567890', 'user': {'id': 42}}
```
```

### Define default values with Field keyword arguments for pyright

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/integrations/visual_studio_code.md

Passes `default` as an explicit keyword argument to `Field` so Pylance/pyright can correctly infer the field is optional. Using positional arguments works at runtime but causes static type checker errors due to dataclass transform limitations.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class Knight(BaseModel):
    title: str = Field(default='Sir Lancelot')  # this is okay
    age: int = Field(
        23
    )  # this works fine at runtime but will case an error for pyright


lance = Knight()  # error: Argument missing for parameter "age"
```

### create_model

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/models.md

Dynamically creates a Pydantic model class using runtime information. Field definitions are provided as keyword arguments, where each value is either a type annotation or a two-tuple of (type, default/Field). Special keyword arguments __config__, __base__, __namespace__, and __module__ customize the new model.

```APIDOC
## create_model

### Description
Dynamically creates a Pydantic model class using runtime information. Field definitions are provided as keyword arguments, where each value is either a type annotation or a two-tuple of (type, default/Field). Special keyword arguments `__config__`, `__base__`, `__namespace__`, and `__module__` customize the new model.

### Method
`create_model(model_name, **field_definitions)`

### Parameters
- **model_name** (str) - Required - The name of the model to create.
- **field_definitions** (keyword arguments) - Required - Each keyword argument defines a field. The value can be:
  - A single element representing the type annotation of the field.
  - A two-tuple where the first element is the type and the second element is the assigned value (either a default or the `Field()` function).
- **__config__** (optional) - A configuration class to customize the new model.
- **__base__** (optional) - A base model class to extend with extra fields.
- **__namespace__** (optional) - A dictionary of attributes (e.g., validators, computed fields, methods) to add to the class namespace. Keys must not clash with field names.
- **__module__** (optional) - The module name to assign to the model (required for pickling).

### Request Example
```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, create_model

DynamicFoobarModel = create_model('DynamicFoobarModel', foo=str, bar=(int, 123))
```

### Response
Returns a new model class (subclass of `BaseModel`).

#### Response Example
```python
<class '__main__.DynamicFoobarModel'>
```
```

def bar(self, baz: int) -> str:

        baz: A description of `baz`.

    Returns:
        A description of the return value.

### Define a before model validator with @model_validator(mode='before')

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/validators.md

Runs before model instantiation and receives raw input data as `Any`. Avoid mutating the raw input value directly if raising errors later, as the mutated value may be passed to other validators.

```python
from typing import Any

from pydantic import BaseModel, model_validator


class UserModel(BaseModel):
    username: str

    @model_validator(mode='before')
    @classmethod
    def check_card_number_not_present(cls, data: Any) -> Any:  # (1)!
        if isinstance(data, dict):
            if 'card_number' in data:
                raise ValueError("'card_number' should not be included")
        return data
```

### Demonstrating strict mode and JSON validation with BaseModel

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/why.md

Shows default data coercion with model_validate, strict mode validation failure with strict=True, and valid parsing via model_validate_json.

```python
from datetime import datetime

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError


class Meeting(BaseModel):
    when: datetime
    where: bytes


m = Meeting.model_validate({'when': '2020-01-01T12:00', 'where': 'home'})
print(m)
#> when=datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 1, 12, 0) where=b'home'
try:
    m = Meeting.model_validate(
        {'when': '2020-01-01T12:00', 'where': 'home'}, strict=True
    )
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e)
    """
    2 validation errors for Meeting
    when
      Input should be a valid datetime [type=datetime_type, input_value='2020-01-01T12:00', input_type=str]
    where
      Input should be a valid bytes [type=bytes_type, input_value='home', input_type=str]
    """

m_json = Meeting.model_validate_json(
    '{"when": "2020-01-01T12:00", "where": "home"}'
)
print(m_json)
#> when=datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 1, 12, 0) where=b'home'
```

### Exclude and include specific fields with model_dump()

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/serialization.md

Use `exclude` with a set or dictionary to exclude fields, or `include` to include only specified fields. Using `False` to include a field in `exclude` (or exclude a field in `include`) is not supported.

```python
# using a set:
print(t.model_dump(exclude={'user', 'value'}))
#> {'id': '1234567890'}

# using a dictionary:
print(t.model_dump(exclude={'user': {'username', 'password'}, 'value': True}))
#> {'id': '1234567890', 'user': {'id': 42}}

# same configuration using `include`:
print(t.model_dump(include={'id': True, 'user': {'id'}}))
#> {'id': '1234567890', 'user': {'id': 42}}
```

--------------------------------

### Use standard library dataclasses in BaseModel with instance revalidation

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/dataclasses.md

Use a stdlib dataclass as a field type in a BaseModel with ConfigDict(revalidate_instances='always') to enforce validation on model instantiation.

```python
import dataclasses

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, ValidationError


@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True)
class User:
    name: str


class Foo(BaseModel):
    # Required so that pydantic revalidates the model attributes:
    model_config = ConfigDict(revalidate_instances='always')

    user: User | None = None


# nothing is validated as expected:
user = User(name=['not', 'a', 'string'])
print(user)
#> User(name=['not', 'a', 'string'])


try:
    Foo(user=user)
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e)
    """
    1 validation error for Foo
    user.name
      Input should be a valid string [type=string_type, input_value=['not', 'a', 'string'], input_type=list]
    """

foo = Foo(user=User(name='pika'))
try:
    foo.user.name = 'bulbi'
except dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError as e:
    print(e)
    #> cannot assign to field 'name'
```

--------------------------------

### Demonstrate unexpected type coercion with left_to_right union ordering

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/unions.md

Shows how member ordering in `left_to_right` mode can lead to surprising results in lax mode. A numeric string like `'456'` matches the first member `int` via coercion instead of matching `str`.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class User(BaseModel):
    id: int | str = Field(union_mode='left_to_right')


print(User(id=123))  # (1)
#> id=123
print(User(id='456'))  # (2)
#> id=456
```

### Serializing and Validating Queue Data with Redis and Pydantic

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/examples/queues.md

Demonstrates serializing Pydantic models with model_dump_json() to push into a Redis queue, and deserializing/validating items with model_validate_json() when popping. Requires a locally running Redis server instance.

```python
import redis

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr


class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str
    email: EmailStr


r = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379, db=0)
QUEUE_NAME = 'user_queue'


def push_to_queue(user_data: User) -> None:
    serialized_data = user_data.model_dump_json()
    r.rpush(QUEUE_NAME, serialized_data)
    print(f'Added to queue: {serialized_data}')


user1 = User(id=1, name='John Doe', email='john@example.com')
user2 = User(id=2, name='Jane Doe', email='jane@example.com')

push_to_queue(user1)
#> Added to queue: {"id":1,"name":"John Doe","email":"john@example.com"}

push_to_queue(user2)
#> Added to queue: {"id":2,"name":"Jane Doe","email":"jane@example.com"}


def pop_from_queue() -> None:
    data = r.lpop(QUEUE_NAME)

    if data:
        user = User.model_validate_json(data)
        print(f'Validated user: {repr(user)}')
    else:
        print('Queue is empty')


pop_from_queue()
#> Validated user: User(id=1, name='John Doe', email='john@example.com')

pop_from_queue()
#> Validated user: User(id=2, name='Jane Doe', email='jane@example.com')

pop_from_queue()
#> Queue is empty
```

### Using Pydantic with ARQ job queues

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/examples/queues.md

Demonstrates defining a job data model, serializing it with model_dump for Redis queueing, and validating it with model_validate in an ARQ worker function. Requires a running Redis server instance.

```python
import asyncio
from typing import Any

from arq import create_pool
from arq.connections import RedisSettings

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr


class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str
    email: EmailStr


REDIS_SETTINGS = RedisSettings()


async def process_user(ctx: dict[str, Any], user_data: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    user = User.model_validate(user_data)
    print(f'Processing user: {repr(user)}')


async def enqueue_jobs(redis):
    user1 = User(id=1, name='John Doe', email='john@example.com')
    user2 = User(id=2, name='Jane Doe', email='jane@example.com')

    await redis.enqueue_job('process_user', user1.model_dump())
    print(f'Enqueued user: {repr(user1)}')

    await redis.enqueue_job('process_user', user2.model_dump())
    print(f'Enqueued user: {repr(user2)}')


class WorkerSettings:
    functions = [process_user]
    redis_settings = REDIS_SETTINGS


async def main():
    redis = await create_pool(REDIS_SETTINGS)
    await enqueue_jobs(redis)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    asyncio.run(main())
```

### Benchmark TypedDict vs Nested BaseModel Performance

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/performance.md

Compares validation speed between TypedDict and nested BaseModel structures using TypeAdapter and model_validate.

```python
from timeit import timeit

from typing_extensions import TypedDict

from pydantic import BaseModel, TypeAdapter


class A(TypedDict):
    a: str
    b: int


class TypedModel(TypedDict):
    a: A


class B(BaseModel):
    a: str
    b: int


class Model(BaseModel):
    b: B


ta = TypeAdapter(TypedModel)
result1 = timeit(
    lambda: ta.validate_python({'a': {'a': 'a', 'b': 2}}), number=10000
)
result2 = timeit(
    lambda: Model.model_validate({'b': {'a': 'a', 'b': 2}}), number=10000
)
print(result2 / result1)
```

### Allow extra data with ConfigDict(extra='allow')

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/models.md

Set extra='allow' to store extra data in the __pydantic_extra__ dictionary attribute. If extra were set to 'forbid', providing extra data would fail.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict


class Model(BaseModel):
    x: int

    model_config = ConfigDict(extra='allow')


m = Model(x=1, y='a')  # (1)!
assert m.model_dump() == {'x': 1, 'y': 'a'}
assert m.__pydantic_extra__ == {'y': 'a'}
```

### Modify Core Schema In-Place with __get_pydantic_core_schema__

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/json_schema.md

Call the handler to obtain the default core schema, mutate it in place (e.g., adding constraints like max_length), and return the updated schema. You must return a schema even when mutating in place.

```python
from typing import Annotated, Any

from pydantic_core import ValidationError, core_schema

from pydantic import BaseModel, GetCoreSchemaHandler


class SmallString:
    def __get_pydantic_core_schema__(
        self,
        source: type[Any],
        handler: GetCoreSchemaHandler,
    ) -> core_schema.CoreSchema:
        schema = handler(source)
        assert schema['type'] == 'str'
        schema['max_length'] = 10  # modify in place
        return schema


class MyModel(BaseModel):
    value: Annotated[str, SmallString()]


try:
    MyModel(value='too long!!!!!')
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e)
    """
    1 validation error for MyModel
    value
      String should have at most 10 characters [type=string_too_long, input_value='too long!!!!!', input_type=str]
    """
```

### Define RootModel with list and dict root types

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/models.md

Create custom root types by parametrizing RootModel with a generic type. The root value is passed as the first and only argument to __init__ or model_validate; model_dump_json and model_json_schema operate on the root value.

```python
from pydantic import RootModel

Pets = RootModel[list[str]]
PetsByName = RootModel[dict[str, str]]


print(Pets(['dog', 'cat']))
#> root=['dog', 'cat']
print(Pets(['dog', 'cat']).model_dump_json())
#> ["dog","cat"]
print(Pets.model_validate(['dog', 'cat']))
#> root=['dog', 'cat']
print(Pets.model_json_schema())
"""
{'items': {'type': 'string'}, 'title': 'RootModel[list[str]]', 'type': 'array'}
"""

print(PetsByName({'Otis': 'dog', 'Milo': 'cat'}))
#> root={'Otis': 'dog', 'Milo': 'cat'}
print(PetsByName({'Otis': 'dog', 'Milo': 'cat'}).model_dump_json())
#> {"Otis":"dog","Milo":"cat"}
print(PetsByName.model_validate({'Otis': 'dog', 'Milo': 'cat'}))
#> root={'Otis': 'dog', 'Milo': 'cat'}
```

### Validate INI configuration file data with Pydantic

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/examples/files.md

Read an INI file using configparser.ConfigParser and validate a target section with Person.model_validate.

```ini
[PERSON]
name = John Doe

email = john@example.com
```

```python
import configparser

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, PositiveInt


class Person(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: PositiveInt
    email: EmailStr


config = configparser.ConfigParser()
config.read('person.ini')
person = Person.model_validate(config['PERSON'])

### Serialize subclass fields with polymorphic_serialization runtime setting

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/serialization.md

Defines a base model `User` and subclass `UserLogin`, then serializes an `OuterModel` containing a `UserLogin` instance. Without the runtime flag, only base fields are dumped; with `polymorphic_serialization=True`, subclass fields such as `password` are included.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel


class User(BaseModel):  # (1)!
    name: str


class UserLogin(User):
    password: str


class OuterModel(BaseModel):
    user: User


outer_model = OuterModel(
    user=UserLogin(name='pydantic', password='password'),
)


print(outer_model.model_dump())  # (2)!
#> {'user': {'name': 'pydantic'}}
print(outer_model.model_dump(polymorphic_serialization=True))  # (3)!
#> {'user': {'name': 'pydantic', 'password': 'password'}}
```

### Define nested models with Foo, Bar, and Spam

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/models.md

Use models as field types to build hierarchical data. Instantiate Spam with nested dicts; printing shows the model representation, and model_dump() returns a nested dict.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel


class Foo(BaseModel):
    count: int
    size: float | None = None


class Bar(BaseModel):
    apple: str = 'x'
    banana: str = 'y'


class Spam(BaseModel):
    foo: Foo
    bars: list[Bar]


m = Spam(foo={'count': 4}, bars=[{'apple': 'x1'}, {'apple': 'x2'}])
print(m)
"""
foo=Foo(count=4, size=None) bars=[Bar(apple='x1', banana='y'), Bar(apple='x2', banana='y')]
"""
print(m.model_dump())
"""
{
    'foo': {'count': 4, 'size': None},
    'bars': [{'apple': 'x1', 'banana': 'y'}, {'apple': 'x2', 'banana': 'y'}],
}
"""
```

### Serialize and publish messages to RabbitMQ with model_dump_json

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/examples/queues.md

Requires a running RabbitMQ server on localhost. Serializes Pydantic model instances into JSON strings and publishes them to the specified queue using pika.

```python
import pika

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr


class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str
    email: EmailStr


connection = pika.BlockingConnection(pika.ConnectionParameters('localhost'))
channel = connection.channel()
QUEUE_NAME = 'user_queue'
channel.queue_declare(queue=QUEUE_NAME)


def push_to_queue(user_data: User) -> None:
    serialized_data = user_data.model_dump_json()
    channel.basic_publish(
        exchange='',
        routing_key=QUEUE_NAME,
        body=serialized_data,
    )
    print(f'Added to queue: {serialized_data}')


user1 = User(id=1, name='John Doe', email='john@example.com')
user2 = User(id=2, name='Jane Doe', email='jane@example.com')

push_to_queue(user1)
#> Added to queue: {"id":1,"name":"John Doe","email":"john@example.com"}

push_to_queue(user2)
#> Added to queue: {"id":2,"name":"Jane Doe","email":"jane@example.com"}

connection.close()
```

### Configure fields using dataclasses.field and Pydantic Field

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/dataclasses.md

Pydantic dataclasses support both standard library dataclasses.field and Pydantic's Field for metadata, default values, and constraint validation.

```python
import dataclasses

from pydantic import Field
from pydantic.dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class User:
    id: int
    name: str = 'John Doe'
    friends: list[int] = dataclasses.field(default_factory=lambda: [0])
    age: int | None = dataclasses.field(
        default=None,
        metadata={'title': 'The age of the user', 'description': 'do not lie!'},
    )
    height: int | None = Field(
        default=None, title='The height in cm', ge=50, le=300
    )


user = User(id='42', height='250')
print(user)
#> User(id=42, name='John Doe', friends=[0], age=None, height=250)
```

### Create a generic model with TypeVar and Generic (Python 3.10+)

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/models.md

Declare a TypeVar and a model inheriting from BaseModel and Generic to build a reusable Response wrapper. Parametrizing with a concrete type validates data, and invalid input raises ValidationError.

```python
from typing import Generic, TypeVar

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

DataT = TypeVar('DataT')  # (1)!


class DataModel(BaseModel):
    number: int


class Response(BaseModel, Generic[DataT]):  # (2)!
    data: DataT  # (3)!


print(Response[int](data=1))
#> data=1
print(Response[str](data='value'))
#> data='value'
print(Response[str](data='value').model_dump())
#> {'data': 'value'}

data = DataModel(number=1)
print(Response[DataModel](data=data).model_dump())
#> {'data': {'number': 1}}
try:
    Response[int](data='value')
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e)
    """
    1 validation error for Response[int]
    data
      Input should be a valid integer, unable to parse string as an integer [type=int_parsing, input_value='value', input_type=str]
    """
```

### Define models for exclude/include serialization parameters

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/serialization.md

Models used to demonstrate the `exclude` and `include` parameters of `model_dump()`. The `Transaction` model has a field with `exclude=True`.

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, SecretStr


class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    username: str
    password: SecretStr


class Transaction(BaseModel):
    id: str
    private_id: str = Field(exclude=True)
    user: User
    value: int


t = Transaction(
    id='1234567890',
    private_id='123',
    user=User(id=42, username='JohnDoe', password='hashedpassword'),
    value=9876543210,
)
```

### Compare JSON serialization between Pydantic V1 and V2

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/migration.md

Demonstrates the difference in JSON serialization between V1 .json() and V2 .model_dump_json(). V2 outputs compact JSON without spaces by default, which matches json.dumps with custom compact separators.

```python
import json

from pydantic import BaseModel as V2BaseModel
from pydantic.v1 import BaseModel as V1BaseModel


class V1Model(V1BaseModel):
    a: list[str]


class V2Model(V2BaseModel):
    a: list[str]


v1_model = V1Model(a=['fancy', 'sushi'])
v2_model = V2Model(a=['fancy', 'sushi'])

# V1
print(v1_model.json())
#> {"a": ["fancy", "sushi"]}

# V2
print(v2_model.model_dump_json())
#> {"a":["fancy","sushi"]}

# Plain json.dumps
print(json.dumps(v2_model.model_dump()))
#> {"a": ["fancy", "sushi"]}

# Modified json.dumps
print(json.dumps(v2_model.model_dump(), separators=(',', ':')))
#> {"a":["fancy","sushi"]}
```

### Describe function parameters with Field and validate_call

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/validation_decorator.md

Use Annotated with Field for required parameters or set Field as a default value to provide metadata and validation constraints on decorated function arguments.

```python
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import Field, ValidationError, validate_call


@validate_call
def how_many(num: Annotated[int, Field(gt=10)]):
    return num


try:
    how_many(1)
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e)
    """
    1 validation error for how_many
    0
      Input should be greater than 10 [type=greater_than, input_value=1, input_type=int]
    """


@validate_call
def return_value(value: str = Field(default='default value')):
    return value


print(return_value())
#> default value
```

### Triggering 'config-both' Error

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/errors/usage_errors.md

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, PydanticUserError

        a: str

### Parse and validate XML file data using ElementTree and Pydantic

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/examples/files.md

Parse an XML document root into a tag-to-text dictionary using xml.etree.ElementTree and validate it into a Pydantic model.

```xml
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<person>
    <name>John Doe</name>
    <age>30</age>
    <email>john@example.com</email>
</person>
```

```python
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, PositiveInt


class Person(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: PositiveInt
    email: EmailStr


tree = ET.parse('person.xml').getroot()
data = {child.tag: child.text for child in tree}
person = Person.model_validate(data)
print(person)
#> name='John Doe' age=30 email='john@example.com'
```

### Customize $ref references using ref_template

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/json_schema.md

Specify a custom prefix format for `$ref` definitions using the `ref_template` parameter in `json_schema()` or `model_json_schema()`. Definitions remain stored under `$defs` while referencing the custom schema path format.

```python
import json

from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic.type_adapter import TypeAdapter


class Foo(BaseModel):
    a: int


class Model(BaseModel):
    a: Foo


adapter = TypeAdapter(Model)

print(
    json.dumps(
        adapter.json_schema(ref_template='#/components/schemas/{model}'),
        indent=2,
    )
)
"""
{
  "$defs": {
    "Foo": {
      "properties": {
        "a": {
          "title": "A",
          "type": "integer"
        }
      },
      "required": [
        "a"
      ],
      "title": "Foo",
      "type": "object"
    }
  },
  "properties": {
    "a": {
      "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Foo"
    }
  },
  "required": [
    "a"
  ],
  "title": "Model",
  "type": "object"
}
"""
```

### Serialize a subclass of a supported type using its superclass format

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/serialization.md

Subclasses of supported types like date are serialized according to their superclass. Here MyDate is serialized as a standard date, producing ISO format.

```python
from datetime import date

from pydantic import BaseModel


class MyDate(date):
    @property
    def my_date_format(self) -> str:
        return self.strftime('%d/%m/%Y')


class FooModel(BaseModel):
    date: date


m = FooModel(date=MyDate(2023, 1, 1))
print(m.model_dump_json())
#> {"date":"2023-01-01"}
```

### Generate Pydantic models from JSON Schema using datamodel-codegen

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/integrations/datamodel_code_generator.md

Runs datamodel-codegen on a JSON Schema definition file (person.json) to produce typed Pydantic models in model.py.

```bash
datamodel-codegen  --input person.json --input-file-type jsonschema --output model.py

```

```json
{
  "$id": "person.json",
  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "title": "Person",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "first_name": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "The person's first name."
    },
    "last_name": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "The person's last name."
    },
    "age": {
      "description": "Age in years.",
      "type": "integer",
      "minimum": 0
    },
    "pets": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": [
        {
          "$ref": "#/definitions/Pet"
        }
      ]
    },
    "comment": {
      "type": "null"
    }
  },
  "required": [
      "first_name",
      "last_name"
  ],
  "definitions": {
    "Pet": {
      "properties": {
        "name": {
          "type": "string"
        },
        "age": {
          "type": "integer"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

```

```python
# generated by datamodel-codegen:
#   filename:  person.json
#   timestamp: 2020-05-19T15:07:31+00:00
from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, conint


class Pet(BaseModel):
    name: str | None = None
    age: int | None = None


class Person(BaseModel):
    first_name: str = Field(description="The person's first name.")
    last_name: str = Field(description="The person's last name.")
    age: conint(ge=0) | None = Field(None, description='Age in years.')
    pets: list[Pet] | None = None
    comment: Any | None = None

```

### Ignore validation errors in last element with experimental_allow_partial

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/experimental.md

Demonstrates parsing incomplete JSON streams by setting experimental_allow_partial=True in validate_json. All validation errors occurring in the incomplete final element are ignored, returning valid instances for preceding complete items.

```python
from typing import Annotated

from annotated_types import MinLen

from pydantic import BaseModel, TypeAdapter


class MyModel(BaseModel):
    a: int
    b: Annotated[str, MinLen(5)]


ta = TypeAdapter(list[MyModel])
v = ta.validate_json(
    '[{"a": 1, "b": "12345"}, {"a": 1,',
    experimental_allow_partial=True,
)
print(v)
#> [MyModel(a=1, b='12345')]
```

### Using Pydantic with SQLAlchemy Models via from_attributes and Field Aliases

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/examples/orms.md

Demonstrates mapping a SQLAlchemy ORM table instance to a Pydantic model using `ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)`. Aliases are used on fields to prevent conflicts with reserved SQLAlchemy names like `metadata`.

```python
import sqlalchemy as sa
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field


class MyModel(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)

    metadata: dict[str, str] = Field(alias='metadata_')


Base = declarative_base()


class MyTableModel(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'my_table'
    id = sa.Column('id', sa.Integer, primary_key=True)
    # 'metadata' is reserved by SQLAlchemy, hence the '_'
    metadata_ = sa.Column('metadata', sa.JSON)


sql_model = MyTableModel(metadata_={'key': 'val'}, id=1)
pydantic_model = MyModel.model_validate(sql_model)

print(pydantic_model.model_dump())
#> {'metadata': {'key': 'val'}}
print(pydantic_model.model_dump(by_alias=True))
#> {'metadata_': {'key': 'val'}}
```

### Generate JSON schema for union of BaseModel types using TypeAdapter

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/json_schema.md

Generate a unified JSON schema for combinations of BaseModel classes wrapped in a TypeAdapter using union typing.

```python
import json

from pydantic import BaseModel, TypeAdapter


class Cat(BaseModel):
    name: str
    color: str


class Dog(BaseModel):
    name: str
    breed: str


ta = TypeAdapter(Cat | Dog)
ta_schema = ta.json_schema()
print(json.dumps(ta_schema, indent=2))
"""
{
  "$defs": {
    "Cat": {
      "properties": {
        "name": {
          "title": "Name",
          "type": "string"
        },
        "color": {
          "title": "Color",
          "type": "string"
        }
      },
      "required": [
        "name",
        "color"
      ],
      "title": "Cat",
      "type": "object"
    },
    "Dog": {
      "properties": {
        "name": {
          "title": "Name",
          "type": "string"
        },
        "breed": {
          "title": "Breed",
          "type": "string"
        }
      },
      "required": [
        "name",
        "breed"
      ],
      "title": "Dog",
      "type": "object"
    }
  },
  "anyOf": [
    {
      "$ref": "#/$defs/Cat"
    },
    {
      "$ref": "#/$defs/Dog"
    }
  ]
}
"""
```

### Demonstrate annotation resolution inconsistency in nested scopes

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/internals/resolving_annotations.md

Illustrates how backwards compatibility namespace injection can cause dataclass annotations outside a function to unexpectedly resolve against the function's local namespace.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

from pydantic import BaseModel


@dataclass
class Foo:
    # `a` and `b` shouldn't resolve:
    a: 'Model'
    b: 'Inner'


def func():
    Inner = int

    class Model(BaseModel):
        foo: Foo

    Model.__pydantic_complete__
    #> True, should be False.
```

### Add validation, serialization, and JSON schema markers to Annotated types

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/types.md

Apply AfterValidator, PlainSerializer, and WithJsonSchema to customize validation logic, JSON export format, and schema generation for an arbitrary type.

```python
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import (
    AfterValidator,
    PlainSerializer,
    TypeAdapter,
    WithJsonSchema,
)

TruncatedFloat = Annotated[
    float,
    AfterValidator(lambda x: round(x, 1)),
    PlainSerializer(lambda x: f'{x:.1e}', return_type=str),
    WithJsonSchema({'type': 'string'}, mode='serialization'),
]


ta = TypeAdapter(TruncatedFloat)

input = 1.02345
assert input != 1.0

assert ta.validate_python(input) == 1.0

assert ta.dump_json(input) == b'"1.0e+00"'

assert ta.json_schema(mode='validation') == {'type': 'number'}
assert ta.json_schema(mode='serialization') == {'type': 'string'}
```

### Handle third-party types using __get_pydantic_core_schema__ and typing.Annotated

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/types.md

Defines custom core and JSON schema hooks on an annotation class to validate, serialize, and document third-party types in Pydantic models. Integrates with typing.Annotated so existing third-party classes can be parsed from raw inputs or accepted as instances.

```python
from typing import Annotated, Any

from pydantic_core import core_schema

from pydantic import (
    BaseModel,
    GetCoreSchemaHandler,
    GetJsonSchemaHandler,
    ValidationError,
)
from pydantic.json_schema import JsonSchemaValue


class ThirdPartyType:
    """
    This is meant to represent a type from a third-party library that wasn't designed with Pydantic
    integration in mind, and so doesn't have a `pydantic_core.CoreSchema` or anything.
    """

    x: int

    def __init__(self):
        self.x = 0


class _ThirdPartyTypePydanticAnnotation:
    @classmethod
    def __get_pydantic_core_schema__(
        cls,
        _source_type: Any,
        _handler: GetCoreSchemaHandler,
    ) -> core_schema.CoreSchema:
        """
        We return a pydantic_core.CoreSchema that behaves in the following ways:

        * ints will be parsed as `ThirdPartyType` instances with the int as the x attribute
        * `ThirdPartyType` instances will be parsed as `ThirdPartyType` instances without any changes
        * Nothing else will pass validation
        * Serialization will always return just an int
        """

        def validate_from_int(value: int) -> ThirdPartyType:
            result = ThirdPartyType()
            result.x = value
            return result

        from_int_schema = core_schema.chain_schema(
            [
                core_schema.int_schema(),
                core_schema.no_info_plain_validator_function(validate_from_int),
            ]
        )

        return core_schema.json_or_python_schema(
            json_schema=from_int_schema,
            python_schema=core_schema.union_schema(
                [
                    # check if it's an instance first before doing any further work
                    core_schema.is_instance_schema(ThirdPartyType),
                    from_int_schema,
                ]
            ),
            serialization=core_schema.plain_serializer_function_ser_schema(
                lambda instance: instance.x
            ),
        )

    @classmethod
    def __get_pydantic_json_schema__(
        cls, _core_schema: core_schema.CoreSchema, handler: GetJsonSchemaHandler
    ) -> JsonSchemaValue:
        # Use the same schema that would be used for `int`
        return handler(core_schema.int_schema())


# We now create an `Annotated` wrapper that we'll use as the annotation for fields on `BaseModel`s, etc.
PydanticThirdPartyType = Annotated[
    ThirdPartyType, _ThirdPartyTypePydanticAnnotation
]


# Create a model class that uses this annotation as a field
class Model(BaseModel):
    third_party_type: PydanticThirdPartyType


# Demonstrate that this field is handled correctly, that ints are parsed into `ThirdPartyType`, and that
# these instances are also "dumped" directly into ints as expected.
m_int = Model(third_party_type=1)
assert isinstance(m_int.third_party_type, ThirdPartyType)
assert m_int.third_party_type.x == 1
assert m_int.model_dump() == {'third_party_type': 1}

# Do the same thing where an instance of ThirdPartyType is passed in
instance = ThirdPartyType()
assert instance.x == 0
instance.x = 10

m_instance = Model(third_party_type=instance)
assert isinstance(m_instance.third_party_type, ThirdPartyType)
assert m_instance.third_party_type.x == 10
assert m_instance.model_dump() == {'third_party_type': 10}

# Demonstrate that validation errors are raised as expected for invalid inputs
try:
    Model(third_party_type='a')
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e)
    """
    2 validation errors for Model
    third_party_type.is-instance[ThirdPartyType]
      Input should be an instance of ThirdPartyType [type=is_instance_of, input_value='a', input_type=str]
    third_party_type.chain[int,function-plain[validate_from_int()]]
      Input should be a valid integer, unable to parse string as an integer [type=int_parsing, input_value='a', input_type=str]
    """


assert Model.model_json_schema() == {
    'properties': {
        'third_party_type': {'title': 'Third Party Type', 'type': 'integer'}
    },
    'required': ['third_party_type'],
    'title': 'Model',
    'type': 'object',
}
```

### Composing validation, constraints, and transformations using validate_as

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/experimental.md

Defines field pipelines in a Pydantic model using `validate_as` to combine string normalization, numeric bounds, regex pattern constraints, predicate functions, and logical OR operations across types.

```python
from __future__ import annotations

from datetime import datetime
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic.experimental.pipeline import validate_as


class User(BaseModel):
    name: Annotated[str, validate_as(str).str_lower()]  # (1)!
    age: Annotated[int, validate_as(int).gt(0)]  # (2)!
    username: Annotated[str, validate_as(str).str_pattern(r'[a-z]+')]  # (3)!
    password: Annotated[
        str,
        validate_as(str)
        .transform(str.lower)
        .predicate(lambda x: x != 'password'),  # (4)!
    ]
    favorite_number: Annotated[  # (5)!
        int,
        (validate_as(int) | validate_as(str).str_strip().validate_as(int)).gt(
            0
        ),
    ]
    friends: Annotated[list[User], validate_as(...).len(0, 100)]  # (6)!
    bio: Annotated[
        datetime,
        validate_as(int)
        .transform(lambda x: x / 1_000_000)
        .validate_as(...),  # (7)!
    ]
```

### Structural pattern matching on a Pydantic model

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/models.md

Uses Python 3.10 match-case (PEP 636) to match a model's field value and bind the name. Note that match-case is syntactic sugar for attribute access and comparison, not model creation.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel


class Pet(BaseModel):
    name: str
    species: str


a = Pet(name='Bones', species='dog')

match a:
    # match `species` to 'dog', declare and initialize `dog_name`
    case Pet(species='dog', name=dog_name):
        print(f'{dog_name} is a dog')
#> Bones is a dog
    # default case
    case _:
        print('No dog matched')
```

### Postponing Annotation Evaluation with PEP 563 Future Import

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/internals/resolving_annotations.md

Enabling `from __future__ import annotations` automatically stringifies annotations at runtime, allowing references to types defined later in the module.

```python
from __future__ import annotations

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Foo(BaseModel):
    f: MyType
    # Given the future import above, this is equivalent to:
    # f: 'MyType'


type MyType = int

print(Foo.__annotations__)
#> {'f': 'MyType'}
```

### Compare lax and strict mode validation with model_validate()

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/strict_mode.md

Shows the difference in validation behavior between lax mode and strict mode. Passing `strict=True` to `model_validate()` prevents type coercion and raises a `ValidationError` when input types do not match.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError


class MyModel(BaseModel):
    x: int


print(MyModel.model_validate({'x': '123'}))  # lax mode
#> x=123

try:
    MyModel.model_validate({'x': '123'}, strict=True)  # strict mode
except ValidationError as exc:
    print(exc)
    """
    1 validation error for MyModel
    x
      Input should be a valid integer [type=int_type, input_value='123', input_type=str]
    """
```

### Compare attribute copying between a plain class and a BaseModel

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/models.md

Shows that arguments passed to a BaseModel constructor are copied during validation, so the list's id differs from the original. The plain class C1 keeps the same list reference, while C2's arr is a copy.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel


class C1:
    arr = []

    def __init__(self, in_arr):
        self.arr = in_arr


class C2(BaseModel):
    arr: list[int]


arr_orig = [1, 9, 10, 3]


c1 = C1(arr_orig)
c2 = C2(arr=arr_orig)
print(f'{id(c1.arr) == id(c2.arr)=}')
#> id(c1.arr) == id(c2.arr)=False
```

### Compare bound vs unbound type variable serialization permutations

Source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/main/docs/concepts/models.md

Enumerates all permutations of bound specification and generic parametrization. Calling model_dump() on any of the instances yields {'item': {'value': 3}}.

```python
from typing import Generic, TypeVar

from pydantic import BaseModel

TBound = TypeVar('TBound', bound=BaseModel)
TNoBound = TypeVar('TNoBound')


class IntValue(BaseModel):
    value: int


class ItemBound(BaseModel, Generic[TBound]):
    item: TBound


class ItemNoBound(BaseModel, Generic[TNoBound]):
    item: TNoBound


item_bound_inferred = ItemBound(item=IntValue(value=3))
item_bound_explicit = ItemBound[IntValue](item=IntValue(value=3))
item_no_bound_inferred = ItemNoBound(item=IntValue(value=3))
item_no_bound_explicit = ItemNoBound[IntValue](item=IntValue(value=3))

# calling `print(x.model_dump())` on any of the above instances results in the following:
#> {'item': {'value': 3}}
```

# module1.py:

    class Model(BaseModel, Base):
        type LocalType = bytes
